title: Private Pilot Airplane
note: Questions and choices are reproduced from the FAA sample-question document (a U.S. Government work). The FAA document has no answer key: answers and explanations are written by OpenChecklists and cite FAA sources.

questions.stem: Maintenance records show the last transponder inspection was performed on September 1, 2014. The next inspection will be due no later than
questions.explanation: Transponders must have been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months. Calendar months run to the end of the month, so an inspection on September 1, 2014 stays current through September 30, 2016.

questions.stem: With respect to the certification of airmen, which are categories of aircraft?

choices.C: Single-engine land and sea, multiengine land and sea.

questions.explanation: For airman certification, "category" means a broad classification of aircraft: airplane, rotorcraft, glider and lighter-than-air (powered-lift, powered parachute and weight-shift-control are also categories). Gyroplane and helicopter are classes within rotorcraft; single- and multiengine land/sea are classes within airplane.

questions.stem: A flashing white light signal from the control tower to a taxiing aircraft is an indication to

choices.B: taxi only on taxiways and not cross runways.
choices.C: return to the starting point on the airport.

questions.explanation: A flashing white light from the tower applies only to aircraft on the ground and means "return to starting point on airport."

questions.stem: During operations outside controlled airspace at altitudes of more than 1,200 feet AGL, but less than 10,000 feet MSL, the minimum flight visibility for day VFR flight is
questions.explanation: In Class G airspace more than 1,200 feet AGL but below 10,000 feet MSL, day VFR requires 1 statute mile flight visibility (with 500 below, 1,000 above and 2,000 feet horizontal cloud clearance).

questions.stem: Unless otherwise authorized, two-way radio communications with Air Traffic Control are required for landings or takeoffs at all towered airports

choices.B: only when weather conditions are less than VFR.
choices.C: within Class D airspace only when weather conditions are less than VFR.

questions.explanation: Two-way radio communication with the tower must be established before operating to, from or through an airport with an operating control tower, whatever the weather. It is an equipment and communications rule, not a weather minimum.

questions.stem: During operations outside controlled airspace at altitudes of more than 1,200 feet AGL, but less than 10,000 feet MSL, the minimum distance below clouds requirement for VFR flight at night is
questions.explanation: At night in Class G airspace above 1,200 feet AGL and below 10,000 feet MSL, the minimums are 3 statute miles visibility and 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.

questions.stem: Two-way radio communication must be established with the Air Traffic Control facility having jurisdiction over the area prior to entering which class airspace?
questions.explanation: Class C requires two-way radio communication with the ATC facility providing air traffic services before entering. Class E and G have no such requirement for VFR traffic (except Class E/G surface areas around towered airports, which fall under Class D-style tower rules).

questions.stem: Pre-takeoff briefing of passengers about the use of seat belts for a flight is the responsibility of
questions.explanation: The pilot in command must ensure each person on board is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten the safety belt and, if installed, the shoulder harness.

questions.stem: A 100-hour inspection was due at 3302.5 hours. The 100-hour inspection was actually done at 3309.5 hours. When is the next 100-hour inspection due?
questions.explanation: The 100-hour limit may be exceeded by up to 10 hours only to reach a place where the inspection can be done, and any excess time counts against the next interval. The inspection was due at 3302.5, so the next is due at 3302.5 + 100 = 3402.5 hours.

questions.stem: When speaking to a flight service weather briefer, you should state

choices.A: the pilot in command`s full name and address.
choices.C: whether the flight is VFR or IFR.

questions.explanation: When requesting a briefing, tell the briefer you are a pilot and give the information the briefer needs to tailor it, starting with the type of flight planned (VFR or IFR), aircraft identification and type, departure point, route and destination.

questions.stem: Why is frost considered hazardous to flight?

choices.A: Frost changes the basic aerodynamic shape of the airfoils, thereby increasing lift.
choices.B: Frost slows the airflow over the airfoils, thereby increasing control effectiveness.
choices.C: Frost spoils the smooth flow of air over the wings, thereby decreasing lifting capability.

questions.explanation: Frost roughens the wing surface and disrupts the smooth boundary-layer airflow, so the wing stalls at a lower angle of attack and produces less lift. It must be removed before flight.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 5-26, Aerodynamics of Flight
Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 12-15, Weather Theory

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 17.) What wind is forecast for STL at 12,000 feet?
questions.explanation: In the winds-aloft forecast, STL at 12,000 feet reads 2339-04: wind from 230° true at 39 knots, temperature -4 °C. Winds aloft forecasts are always referenced to true north.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 13, Aviation Weather Services

questions.stem: The mature stage of a thunderstorm begins with
questions.explanation: A thunderstorm reaches the mature stage when the drops become too heavy for the updrafts to support and precipitation begins to fall, creating the downdrafts that make this the most violent stage.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 12-22, Weather Theory

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figures 32 and 33.) Which action can adjust the airplane`s weight to maximum gross weight and the CG within limits for takeoff? Front seat occupants: 425 lb Rear seat occupants: 300 lb Fuel, main tanks: 44 gal

choices.C: Transfer 12 gallons of fuel from the main tanks to the auxiliary tanks.

questions.explanation: Empty weight 2,015 lb + front 425 + rear 300 + 44 gal fuel (264 lb) = 3,004 lb, 54 lb over the 2,950 lb maximum. Fuel weighs 6 lb/gal, so draining 9 gallons brings the airplane exactly to 2,950 lb. The new moment (1,554 + 361.3 + 363 + 158 = 2,436.3) falls inside the 2,422–2,499 limits for 2,950 lb. Transferring fuel would not reduce weight.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, Weight and Balance

questions.stem: What action should a pilot take when operating under VFR in a Military Operations Area (MOA)?

choices.A: Obtain a clearance from the controlling agency prior to entering the MOA.
choices.B: Operate only on the airways that transverse the MOA.
choices.C: Exercise extreme caution when military activity is being conducted.

questions.explanation: MOAs separate military training from IFR traffic, but VFR pilots may fly through them without a clearance. Exercise extreme caution while military activity is being conducted, and contact the controlling agency or flight service for traffic advisories.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 15, Airspace

questions.stem: Unless otherwise authorized, if flying a transponder equipped aircraft, a pilot should squawk which VFR code?
questions.explanation: Code 1200 is the VFR code when you are not assigned another. 7600 is lost communications and 7700 is emergency.

questions.stem: What is one purpose of wing flaps?

choices.A: To enable the pilot to make steeper approaches to a landing without increasing the airspeed.
choices.B: To relieve the pilot of maintaining continuous pressure on the controls.
choices.C: To decrease wing area to vary the lift.

questions.explanation: Extending flaps increases lift and drag, allowing a steeper approach without an increase in airspeed and a slower touchdown.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 6, Flight Controls

questions.stem: With regard to carburetor ice, float-type carburetor systems in comparison to fuel injection systems are generally considered to be
questions.explanation: Float-type carburetors are more susceptible to icing than fuel-injection systems because fuel vaporization and the venturi pressure drop cool the air in the carburetor throat. Fuel-injection systems have no venturi in which this ice can form.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 7, Aircraft Systems

questions.stem: What does the red line on an airspeed indicator represent?
questions.explanation: The red radial line marks VNE, the never-exceed speed. Operating above it may cause structural damage or failure.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 8, Flight Instruments

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 48.) The portion of the runway identified by the letter A may be used for
questions.explanation: The arrows at A mark a displaced threshold. That part of the runway is available for taxiing, takeoff and the landing rollout from the opposite direction, but not for landing in this direction.

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 47.) While on final approach to a runway equipped with a standard 2-bar VASI, the lights appear as shown by illustration D. This means that the aircraft is
questions.explanation: On a two-bar VASI, all red (illustration D) means the aircraft is below the glide path. Red over white is on the glide path; all white is above it.

questions.stem: Who has final authority to accept or decline any land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance?
questions.explanation: The pilot in command has final authority to accept or decline any land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance. Decline it if you have any doubt that you can safely stop or hold short.

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 38.) Determine the approximate landing ground roll distance. Pressure altitude: 5,000 ft Headwind: Calm Temperature: 101°F
questions.explanation: At 5,000 feet and 41 °F the table gives a 495-foot ground roll. 101 °F is 60 °F hotter than that, and note 2 adds 10% for each 60 °F above standard: 495 × 1.10 ≈ 545 feet.

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 38.) Determine the total distance required to land over a 50-foot obstacle. Pressure altitude: 5,000 ft Headwind: 8 kts Temperature: 41°F Runway: Hard surface
questions.explanation: The table gives 1,195 feet to clear a 50-foot obstacle at 5,000 feet and 41 °F. Note 1 subtracts 10% for each 4 knots of headwind, so 8 knots means 20%: 1,195 × 0.80 = 956 feet.

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 35.) Determine the approximate manifold pressure setting with 2,450 RPM to achieve 65 percent maximum continuous power at 6,500 feet with a temperature of 36°F higher than standard.
questions.explanation: Use the ISA +20 °C (+36 °F) columns. At 2,450 RPM the manifold pressure is 21.0 in. Hg at 6,000 feet and 20.8 at 8,000 feet. Interpolating to 6,500 feet gives about 20.95, or 21.0 in. Hg.

questions.stem: The term 'angle of attack' is defined as the angle between the

choices.A: chord line of the wing and the relative wind.
choices.B: airplane's longitudinal axis and that of the air striking the airfoil.
choices.C: airplane's center line and the relative wind.

questions.explanation: Angle of attack is the acute angle between the chord line of the airfoil and the direction of the relative wind.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 5-2, Aerodynamics of Flight

questions.stem: When the course deviation indicator (CDI) needle is centered using a VOR test signal (VOT), the omnibearing selector (OBS) and the TO/FROM indicator should read

choices.A: 180° FROM, only if the pilot is due north of the VOT.
choices.B: 0° TO or 180° FROM, regardless of the pilot`s position from the VOT.
choices.C: 0° FROM or 180° TO, regardless of the pilot`s position from the VOT.

questions.explanation: A VOT transmits the 360° radial in all directions. With the CDI centered, the OBS should read 0° with a FROM indication or 180° with a TO indication, wherever you are relative to the VOT.

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 26, area 2.) The day VFR visibility and cloud clearance requirements to operate over the town of Cooperstown, after departing and climbing out of the Cooperstown Airport at or below 700 feet AGL are

choices.B: 1 mile and 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.

questions.explanation: Cooperstown lies inside the magenta vignette, so Class E begins 700 feet AGL. At or below 700 feet AGL you are in Class G, where day VFR below 1,200 feet AGL requires 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 15, Airspace

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 52.) What is the recommended communications procedure for landing at Lincoln Municipal during the hours when the tower is not in operation?

choices.A: Monitor airport traffic and announce your position and intentions on 118.5 MHz.
choices.B: Contact UNICOM on 122.95 MHz for traffic advisories.
choices.C: Monitor ATIS for airport conditions, then announce your position on 122.95 MHz.

questions.explanation: The Chart Supplement lists CTAF 118.5, which is the tower frequency. When the tower is closed, self-announce your position and intentions on 118.5 MHz.

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 25, area 5.) The navigation facility at Dallas-Ft. Worth International (DFW) is a
questions.explanation: The navaid at DFW (AOE) uses the square-with-a-dot symbol, which on sectional charts denotes a VOR/DME.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 16, Navigation

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 52.) Where is Loup City Municipal located in relation to the city?
questions.explanation: The Chart Supplement entry for Loup City Muni reads "1 NW": the airport is about 1 nautical mile northwest of the city.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 14-3, Airport Operations

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 52.) When approaching Lincoln Municipal from the west at noon for the purpose of landing, initial communications should be with
questions.explanation: Lincoln is Class C from 1130–0600Z, which includes local noon. Arriving from the west falls in the 180°–359° sector, so the first call is to Lincoln Approach on 124.0 MHz.

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 64.) Which marking indicates a vehicle lane?
questions.explanation: Marking C (the white solid and dashed lines across the apron) is a vehicle roadway marking. It defines a lane where ground vehicles may cross aircraft movement areas.

questions.stem: A pilot and two passengers landed on a 2,100 foot east-west gravel strip with an elevation of 1,800 feet. The temperature is warmer than expected and after computing the density altitude it is determined the takeoff distance over a 50 foot obstacle is 1,980 feet. The airplane is 75 pounds under gross weight. What would be the best choice?

choices.A: Taking off into the headwind will give the extra climb-out time needed.
choices.B: Try a takeoff without the passengers to make sure the climb is adequate.
choices.C: Wait until the temperature decreases, and recalculate the takeoff performance.

questions.explanation: The computed 1,980-foot obstacle-clearance distance leaves almost no margin on a 2,100-foot gravel strip. Waiting for cooler air lowers the density altitude, so the safe choice is to wait and recompute the takeoff performance.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 4-4, Principles of Flight
Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, Aircraft Performance

questions.stem: If an aircraft is equipped with a fixed-pitch propeller and a float-type carburetor, the first indication of carburetor ice would most likely be

choices.A: a drop in oil temperature and cylinder head temperature.

questions.explanation: With a fixed-pitch propeller, the first sign of carburetor ice is usually a loss of RPM, which may be followed by engine roughness.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 7, Aircraft Systems

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 20, area 1.) The NALF Fentress (NFE) Airport is in what type of airspace?
questions.explanation: Fentress NALF (NFE) sits inside a dashed magenta line, which marks Class E airspace extending to the surface.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 15, Airspace

questions.stem: While on a VFR cross country and not in contact with ATC, what frequency would you use in the event of an emergency?
questions.explanation: 121.5 MHz is the VHF emergency frequency. It is monitored by flight service stations, control towers and many aircraft.

questions.stem: ATC advises, "traffic 12 o'clock." This advisory is relative to your
questions.explanation: Radar traffic advisories use clock positions based on the aircraft's ground track as seen on radar. A pilot holding a wind-correction angle must allow for the difference between heading and track.

questions.stem: Which statement relates to Bernoulli's principle?

choices.A: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
choices.B: An additional upward force is generated as the lower surface of the airfoil deflects air downward.
choices.C: Air traveling faster over the curved upper surface of an airfoil causes lower pressure on the top surface.

questions.explanation: Bernoulli's principle says pressure falls as the speed of a moving fluid rises. Faster airflow over the curved upper surface lowers the pressure there, producing lift. Choice A is Newton's third law.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 4, Principles of Flight

questions.stem: Deviation error of the magnetic compass is caused by

choices.B: certain metals and electrical systems within the aircraft.
choices.C: the difference in location of true north and magnetic north.

questions.explanation: Deviation is caused by magnetic fields inside the aircraft, such as metal parts and electrical equipment. It varies with heading and is shown on the compass correction card. Choice C is variation.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 8-24, Flight Instruments

questions.stem: When executing an emergency approach to land in a single-engine airplane, it is important to maintain a constant glide speed because variations in glide speed will

choices.A: increase the chances of shock cooling the engine.
choices.B: assure the proper descent angle is maintained until entering the flare.
choices.C: nullify all attempts at accuracy in judgment of gliding distance and landing spot.

questions.explanation: In an emergency landing, gliding distance and the landing spot can only be judged accurately at a constant airspeed. Every change in glide speed changes the glide path and spoils that judgment.

cites.label: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 18, Emergency Procedures

questions.stem: How far will an aircraft travel in 7.5 minutes with a ground speed of 114 knots?
questions.explanation: Distance = groundspeed × time: 114 knots × 7.5/60 hours = 14.25 nautical miles.

questions.stem: The radius of the procedural outer area of Class C airspace is normally
questions.explanation: Class C airspace has a procedural outer area, normally with a 20 NM radius, where approach control provides services to participating aircraft.

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 8.) What is the effect of a temperature increase from 35 to 50°F on the density altitude if the pressure altitude remains at 3,000 feet MSL?
questions.explanation: Density altitude rises about 120 feet for each 1 °C of warming. 35 °F is about 1.7 °C and 50 °F is about 10 °C, a rise of about 8.3 °C, so density altitude increases by about 1,000 feet, matching the chart.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 4-4, Principles of Flight

questions.stem: The Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM) specifically encourages pilots to turn on their landing lights when operating below 10,000 feet, day or night, and especially when operating

choices.C: within 15 miles of a towered airport.

questions.explanation: The AIM encourages pilots to turn on landing lights below 10,000 feet, day or night, especially within 10 miles of an airport, in conditions of reduced visibility and where birds may be expected.

questions.stem: When making routine transponder code changes, pilots should avoid inadvertent selection of which code?
questions.explanation: When changing codes, avoid accidentally selecting 7500 (unlawful interference), 7600 (lost communications) or 7700 (emergency), because each one can trigger an alarm at ATC.

questions.stem: A pilot experiencing the effects of hyperventilation should be able to restore the proper carbon dioxide level in the body by

choices.A: slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a paper bag, or talking aloud.
choices.B: breathing spontaneously and deeply or gaining mental control of the situation.
choices.C: increasing the breathing rate in order to increase lung ventilation.

questions.explanation: Hyperventilation is an excessive loss of carbon dioxide. Slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a paper bag or talking aloud restores CO2.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 17-5, Aeromedical Factors

questions.stem: This sign confirms your position on
questions.explanation: Yellow numbers on a black background with a yellow border make a runway location sign. It tells you which runway you are on, here runway 22.

questions.stem: From the cockpit, this marking confirms the aircraft to be

choices.A: on a taxiway, about to enter runway zone.
choices.B: on a runway, about to clear.
choices.C: near an instrument approach clearance zone.

questions.explanation: Holding position markings have two solid and two dashed yellow lines, and the solid lines are always on the side where aircraft hold. Approaching from the dashed side means you are on the runway and about to clear it.

questions.stem: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 78.) What are the basic VFR weather minima required to takeoff from the Onawa, IA (K36) airport during the day?

choices.A: 3 statute miles visibility, 500 feet below the clouds, 1,000 feet above the clouds, and 2,000 feet horizontally from the clouds.

questions.explanation: Onawa (K36) has no magenta vignette or dashed line around it, so the airspace is Class G from the surface up to 1,200 feet AGL. Day VFR there requires 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds.

questions.stem: If Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) capability is lost in-flight,

choices.A: the pilot may still rely on GPS derived altitude for vertical information.
choices.B: the pilot has no assurance of the accuracy of the GPS position.
choices.C: GPS position is reliable provided at least 3 GPS satellites are available.

questions.explanation: RAIM is how the receiver checks the integrity of the satellite signals. Without RAIM there is no assurance that the GPS position is accurate.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 16-31, Navigation

questions.stem: You plan to phone a weather briefing facility for preflight weather information. You should

choices.A: provide the number of occupants on board.
choices.C: begin with your route of flight.

questions.explanation: Begin a weather briefing request by identifying yourself as a pilot, then give the type of flight, aircraft identification and type, route, destination and planned times.

questions.stem: Your cousin wants you to take him flying. You must have made at least three takeoffs and three landings in your aircraft within the preceding
questions.explanation: To carry passengers you must have made three takeoffs and three landings in the preceding 90 days, as sole manipulator of the controls, in an aircraft of the same category, class and (if required) type.

questions.stem: In what flight condition are torque effects more pronounced in a single-engine airplane?

choices.A: Low airspeed, high power, high angle of attack.
choices.B: Low airspeed, low power, low angle of attack.
choices.C: High airspeed, high power, high angle of attack.

questions.explanation: Left-turning tendencies (torque, P-factor and spiraling slipstream) are strongest at low airspeed, high power and high angle of attack, for example during takeoff and climb.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 5, Aerodynamics of Flight

questions.stem: The wind at 5,000 feet AGL is southwesterly while the surface wind is southerly. This difference in direction is primarily due to

choices.A: stronger pressure gradient at higher altitudes.
choices.B: friction between the wind and the surface.
choices.C: stronger Coriolis force at the surface.

questions.explanation: Within about 2,000 feet of the ground, surface friction slows the wind. That weakens the Coriolis force, so surface wind is turned toward lower pressure and differs in direction from the wind aloft.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 12-4, Weather Theory

questions.stem: Eye movements during daytime collision avoidance scanning should

choices.A: not exceed 10 degrees and view each sector at least 1 second.
choices.B: be 30 degrees and view each sector at least 3 seconds.
choices.C: use peripheral vision by scanning small sectors and utilizing off-center viewing.

questions.explanation: Effective daytime scanning uses short, regularly spaced eye movements. Each movement should not exceed 10°, and each area should be viewed for at least 1 second.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 14-28, Airport Operations

questions.stem: When there is a temperature inversion, you would expect to experience

choices.A: clouds with extensive vertical development above an inversion aloft.
choices.B: good visibility in the lower levels of the atmosphere and poor visibility above an inversion aloft.
choices.C: an increase in temperature as altitude increases.

questions.explanation: A temperature inversion is a layer in which temperature increases with altitude instead of decreasing.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 12-13, Weather Theory

questions.stem: When warm, moist, stable air flows upslope, it
questions.explanation: Stable air forced up a slope cools to its dew point but resists vertical development. The result is layered stratus clouds and upslope fog rather than showers.

cites.label: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), p. 12-15, Weather Theory

questions.stem: The correct method of stating 5,500 feet MSL to ATC is
questions.explanation: Below 18,000 feet MSL, state altitudes as the separate digits of the thousands plus the hundreds, for example "FIVE THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED."

questions.stem: Unless otherwise authorized, which situation requires Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B)?

choices.A: Landing at an airport with an operating control tower.
choices.B: Overflying Class C airspace below 10,000 feet MSL.
choices.C: Flying under the shelf of Class C airspace.

questions.explanation: ADS-B Out is required above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of Class B or Class C airspace up to 10,000 feet MSL. Flying under a Class C shelf, outside a Mode C veil, does not require it.

skipped.stem: Each person who holds a pilot certificate or a medical certificate shall present it for inspection upon the request of any
skipped.reason: Ambiguous: 14 CFR 61.3(l) lists both the Administrator and any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer, so more than one choice is supported by the regulation.
